extracted.intended_audience: math teachers and students using classroom-tested combinatorics projects
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze partitions of a square (10x10 board) into four rectangles: define configuration classes under rotation/reflection, model the iterative partitioning as a decision tree, enumerate configuration classes and colorings, and determine minimal guesses/unknowns required to uniquely determine boards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Configuration class definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Two boards are in the same configuration class if they are equivalent under rotation and reflection, without regard to the size, location, and suit of each rectangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: c/ in Figure 3i/ is not equivalent to the others — you cannot rotate, reflect, or “slide” any of the line segments from a/, b/, or d / to produce c/. Use rotation/reflection equivalence only; ignore rectangle sizes, positions, and suits when grouping into classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a full-span border segment
rubrics_metrics.description: Every partition of a square into four rectangles contains at least one vertical or horizontal line segment that forms a border between suits and extends from one edge of the board to the opposite edge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation from Problem 3; the task is to prove this always exists for any partition of a square into four rectangles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partitioning as an iterative three-step process
rubrics_metrics.description: Partitioning the square into four rectangles can be viewed as an iterative process of three steps such that at each step exactly one rectangle is divided into two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First step: divide the square into two rectangles with a vertical or horizontal line. Second: divide one of those rectangles into two (horizontal or vertical). Third: divide one of the three rectangles to produce four. Note that which rectangle is subdivided at each step matters (e.g., dividing A vs B leads to different outcomes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision tree of partitioning choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a decision tree to indicate all possible ways that a board can be divided into four rectangles, accounting for choices (horizontal/vertical and which rectangle to split) at each step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Realize certain decisions are equivalent: a horizontal first line and a vertical first line are indistinguishable because the resulting boards are equivalent under rotation. Partitions are distinguished by the relative positions of the rectangles to one another, but not by the size of the rectangles. Terminal nodes of the tree (after three decisions) represent configuration classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal nodes correspond to configuration classes (counting classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The terminal nodes of the decision tree (i.e., nodes resulting from three decisions) represent configuration classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the decision tree to enumerate how many distinct configuration classes are produced; treat nodes that are equivalent under rotation/reflection as the same class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal number of guesses per configuration class
rubrics_metrics.description: For each configuration class, determine the minimal number of guesses required to complete the board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within a single configuration class, different positions of borders can yield different minimal numbers of guesses. For example, Figure 5 shows boards from the same configuration class that require different minimal numbers (example: 4 guesses vs 6 guesses). Draw representative boards within each class to find all possible minimal-guess counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting all different colorings
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine how many different colorings of the board are possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use configuration classes to guide the count. Realize that two boards in the same configuration class that are equivalent under rotation produce different colorings (i.e., count rotated colorings separately). Also account for different positions of borders and different distributions of suits when counting distinct colorings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum unknown squares to allow multiple completions
rubrics_metrics.description: For a completed board, determine the minimum number of squares that can remain unknown so that more than one board is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples of which specific squares would have to remain unknown to achieve this minimal number (applies to completed boards like those in Figure 6).
